Horayot 3b:13.english: The mishna explains for which type of unwitting transgression based on the ruling of the court there is liability to bring an offering. In a case where the judges of the court issued an erroneous ruling to abolish the entire essence of a mitzva, not only a detail thereof, e.g., they said: There is no prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, or there is no prohibition against performing prohibited labor on Shabbat written in the Torah, or there is no prohibition against engaging in idol worship written in the Torah, these judges are exempt, as this is an error based on ignorance, not an erroneous ruling. If the judges issued a ruling to nullify part of a mitzva and to sustain part of that mitzva, these judges are liable.

Horayot 3b:14.english: How so? An example of this is if the judges said: There is a prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, but one who engages in intercourse with a woman who observes a clean day for a day she experiences a discharge is exempt. When the woman sees a discharge of blood for one or two days during the eleven days between the end of one menstrual period and the expected start of another, the blood is assumed to not be menstrual blood. If after the second day, the next day passes without any discharge of blood, she may immerse immediately and she is ritually pure. The judges ruled erroneously that it is permitted to engage in intercourse with her on the day that she is observing a clean day, even without the day having passed and her having immersed; or if they said:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:11:1.english: The court issued a ruling - And the majority of the public acted according to their ruling:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:11:2.english: And they discovered that they erred and reversed their decision - from their ruling:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:11:3.english: Whether they brought their atonement offering or whether they did not bring their atonement offering - And after they knew that they erred, the individual went and acted according to their ruling, for this does not combine with the majority of the public, because this individual acted after it became known to them:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:11:4.english: Rabbi Shimon deems him exempt - Because he acts with the permission of the court, as this individual still did not know that they (the court) erred and reversed their decision, and he is considered to be relying on the court. Therefore, he is exempt:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:11:5.english: Rabbi Elazar says: Uncertainty - Meaning, it is uncertain whether he is considered to be relying on the court or relying on himself, and he brings a provisional guilt-offering:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:11:6.english: Which is the case of uncertainty - Meaning, why is he liable to bring a provisional guilt-offering:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:11:7.english: If one sat inside his house he is liable - to bring a provisional guilt-offering:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:12:1.english: That he is closer to exemption - For he is certainly considered to be relying on the court, as he did not know of their reversal, since he went to a country overseas:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:12:2.english: Ben Azzai said to him: In what way is this different - The one who went to a country overseas, from one who sits in his house:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:12:3.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him - Because one who sits in his house could possibly hear that the court reversed its decision, and is therefore close to being considered as relying on himself, and is consequently liable to bring a provisional guilt-offering. But this one who went to a country overseas could not hear, and is truly considered to be relying on the court. Therefore, he is exempt:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:1:1.hebrew: או לא בעינן ההוא בית דין דהורו להם מעיקרא דתהוי להו ידיעה - כלומר, לא בעינן דתהוי להו ידיעה לבית דין קמא ומצטרפי:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:2:1.english: “Until the ruling disseminates throughout the entire assembly of Israel” - This refers to those who convened to issue the ruling:

Rashi on Horayot 3b:4:1.english: For example, that one of them bowed his head - or a student, bowed his head, as it appeared that he agreed with their words, and the ruling was finalized.

Rashi on Horayot 3b:7:1.hebrew: במארה אתם נארים וגו' - כגון שהגוי כולו דיכולין לקבלה. הכי משמע: אי איכא גוי כולו וקא עבר עליה האי גברא, אותי אתם קובעים. והכי כתוב בספרים במס' עבודת כוכבים בפ' אין מעמידין:
Rashi on Horayot 3b:7:1.english: “With the curse you are cursed, etc.” - for example, that the entire nation is able to accept it. This is what it means: if there is an entire nation and this person transgresses against it, “you rob Me.” And so it is written in the books in Tractate Avodah Zarah, in the chapter 'Ein Ma'amidin'.

Rashi on Horayot 3b:8:1.english: If all of them are present - the Sanhedrin of seventy-one.

Rashi on Horayot 3b:8:2.english: It is a ruling - even if not all of those who sat to issue the ruling actually issued it.

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3b:1.english: There is room to say that only when the court that issued the ruling itself later retracted and decided that it had erred — then the public brings an offering. But the decision of another court would not have this law, rather the congregation would be considered as if they acted due to the error of individuals.

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3b:11.english: And here it is discussed when the majority of the public acted according to the court's ruling (Rashi). Indeed, the Meiri believes that what emerges from this Mishnah is that it is based on the reasoning that an individual who acted according to the court's ruling is exempt, and not only the first Tanna but also the other Tannaim agree in principle with this view. And he noted that this is the reasoning, even though there is seemingly a contradiction from Tractate Shabbat. And indeed, in Tosafot there (93b), they raised a difficulty from here on Rashi's words there, where Rabbi Shimon holds that an individual who acted according to the court's ruling is liable. However, from Rashi's language here, it can be understood that it refers to an individual who acted in conjunction with the entire public (and see the words of the commentators).

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3b:12.english: The Rosh wonders: The essence of this view is from the words of the Tanna Rabbi Elazar (ben Shamua), who was a student of Rabbi Akiva (and according to the names of the disputing Tannaim, it is clear that it is impossible to read 'Rabbi Eliezer' here), and it is puzzling that Rabbi Akiva would use this language of concession regarding the words of his student. Indeed, the commentators have already brought the version of the Yerushalmi (according to an old reading) where it says "I see" in this place, and this language is appropriate even in the words of a teacher regarding his student (Magen Giborim, Ḥok Natan).

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3b:13.english: A court is never liable unless it issued a ruling to nullify part and sustain part in matters that are not explicitly stated in the Torah. For example, if they erred and said that carrying from one domain to another on Shabbat is prohibited, but passing an object is permitted, or if they said that bowing to an idol without extending one's hands and feet is permitted. This is like an unstated Mishnah and its explanation will be given later in the Gemara. (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:2).

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Horayot 3b:2.english: A similar approach is found in the Yerushalmi, that one hundred judges who sat must all decide as one. There, it further raises a question: Is it enough that all of them decide to permit a prohibited matter, or must they decide based on one reason specifically? In the book B"Sh, a serious question was raised: How is it possible for one hundred to sit and judge? The Great Sanhedrin (which decides on such matters) consists of seventy-one members, and one does not add to them (as it is a scriptural decree, as God told Moses). So how can one hundred judge as a court? It remains unresolved. Some explained that the language is not precise, and it is merely an exaggeration, as there is no court of more than seventy-one (Chak Natan). Others wrote that perhaps it refers to a case where another central court was added to them (such as the court of twenty-three that sat at the entrance of the Temple, which was also a central court), and all of them judged the matter as one (Hora Gever). Others wrote that there were other important students worthy of issuing rulings before the court, who were also among those judging the matter (even if they do not count towards the quorum), and this is also how Rashi's language is interpreted (Zera Avraham). Indeed, some said that even though the Great Sanhedrin is not less than seventy-one, it was possible to add to it for various purposes (Meromei Sadeh), as we find in various places in the Talmud that the Men of the Great Assembly were one hundred and twenty elders who established halakhot for all of Israel (R. Tz. Chayot).

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Horayot 3b:11.english: Meaning, in which case do we have uncertainty whether his status is considered as relying on the court or not (Rabbi Yonatan). And later commentators noted that Rashi's words should also be understood this way.

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Horayot 3b:2.english: Rashi explains that 'until the ruling disseminates throughout the assembly of Israel' means in the session of the Sanhedrin, who are called 'assembly'.

Steinsaltz comment #3 on Horayot 3b:11.english: The court issued a ruling and erred, and afterwards they reversed their decision. And an individual performed an action according to their ruling after their error became known to them — this person brings a provisional guilt-offering. Since he could have asked if anything new had occurred in the court but did not ask, he is like one who is uncertain if he committed a transgression. But if he traveled to a country overseas, even if he performed the action after the error became known to the court — he is exempt, because he relied on them, and it was impossible for him to ask. This is in accordance with the words of Rabbi Elazar, to whom Rabbi Akiva also concedes. (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:5).

Steinsaltz comment #3 on Horayot 3b:2.english: If the court issued a ruling and one of them knew that they erred and told them that they were mistaken, even though those who permitted outnumbered the dissenters and the majority of the public acted according to their ruling—the court is exempt from an offering, and all those who acted are obligated to bring an individual sin-offering. This is in accordance with the words of Rabbi Yonatan (Rambam, Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 13:1).

Steinsaltz comment #4 on Horayot 3b:11.english: A court that erred and ruled to abolish an entire category of Torah law, even if the entire congregation acted according to their ruling — the court is exempt, and each individual who performed the action is liable to bring a sin-offering. This is like an unstated Mishnah. (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:1).

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:21.english: A dilemma was raised before them [it was asked of them, the students]: If the court issued a ruling that forbidden fat is permitted, and a minority of the congregation performed the transgression on its basis, and that court died and another court stood in its place, and again issued the same ruling to permit, and a different minority performed the transgression, what will be the *halakha*?

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3a:22.english: And they elaborate: According to the opinion of the one who says that the court alone brings the offering, do not raise the dilemma [do not ask, do not be in doubt] for yourself — as those judges who ruled and on whose basis the majority of the congregation acted are not here, for the first court has already died. Rather, when you should raise the question for yourself — it is according to the opinion of the one who says that the congregation is the one that brings the offering. If so, what [is the *halakha*]? And the sides of the question are: The congregation exists [stands], for together it is found that a majority of the congregation sinned.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:1.english: Or perhaps [maybe] we require [we need] the awareness of that court that issued the ruling; and that court no longer exists! This question was not resolved and remained as a *teiku* [it shall stand] in its place.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:10.english: It is related that Rav Huna, when he would go out to the court, would bring ten tanna'im of the study hall before him to be as if they were partners with him in judgment, for he would say: So that we will receive a splinter from the beam, meaning, that they would share the responsibility for the ruling with him. Similarly, it is related that Rav Ashi, when they would bring a tereifa before him to ask if the animal was a tereifa or not, would bring ten slaughterers from Mata Meḥasya and seat them before him. He said: So that we will receive a splinter from the beam.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:11.english: MISHNA: The court issued an erroneous ruling, and they discovered that they erred and reversed their decision, whether they brought their atonement (offering) for what they ruled or whether they did not bring their atonement, and a person who did not know that they reversed their decision proceeded and performed a transgression on the basis of their ruling — Rabbi Shimon deems him exempt from an offering, and Rabbi Elazar says: It is uncertainty, and he brings a provisional guilt-offering. Which is the case of uncertainty? When is something considered an uncertainty for which one is liable to bring a provisional guilt-offering? If a person sat inside his house and did so — he is liable to bring a guilt-offering, as he could have known that the court reversed its decision. If he went to a country overseas and is still relying on the old ruling — he is exempt.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:12.english: Rabbi Akiva said: I concede in that case of one who went to a country overseas that he is closer to exemption than to liability. Ben Azzai said to him: In what way is this person different from one who sits in his house? He said to him: That one who sits in his house it would have been possible for him to hear, but this one who is in a country overseas it would not have been possible for him to hear. And from here the Mishnah comes to explain in what matter the thing is considered an erroneous ruling for which the public brings an offering.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:13.english: The court issued a ruling to abolish the entire essence of the mitzvah and not a single detail from it, for example, if they said: There is no prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, there is no prohibition against performing prohibited labor on Shabbat written in the Torah, there is no prohibition against engaging in idol worship written in the Torah — these judges are exempt. For this is not an erroneous ruling but a simple mistake. If they issued a ruling to nullify part of the mitzvah and to sustain part of it — these judges are liable.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:14.english: How so? If they said: There is a prohibition against engaging in intercourse with a menstruating woman written in the Torah, but one who engages in intercourse with a woman who observes a day for a day — referring to a woman who saw menstrual blood not at its regular time for one day, in which case she needs to observe a second day and check if her menstruation continues, and even if she did not see blood on the second day, she is considered a menstruating woman for that day — and they ruled that one who engages in intercourse with her is exempt, or if they said:

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:15.english: There is Shabbat in the Torah, but one who carries out from the private domain to the public domain is exempt.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:16.english: There is idol worship in the Torah, but one who bows (who did not offer a sacrifice to it) is exempt — these judges are liable for an erroneous ruling, as it is stated: “And the matter is hidden” (Leviticus 4:13), to say “a matter” — a single detail, and not the entire essence.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:2.english: Rabbi Yonatan says: Even one hundred judges who sat in judgment to issue a ruling, and they deliberated on the matter and erred—they are not liable to bring an offering until all of them issue the ruling, as it is stated regarding the liability for the offering: “And if the entire assembly of Israel shall act unwittingly” (Leviticus 4:13). The term “entire” comes to emphasize: until all of them act unwittingly, meaning, until the ruling disseminates (is accepted) throughout the entire assembly of Israel, that this erroneous ruling is with the consent of “the entire assembly”—the Sanhedrin. Rav Huna, son of Rav Hoshaya, said: So too it is reasonable to conclude this, as throughout the entire Torah we maintain the principle that its majority is like its entirety, and here it does not say "assembly" alone, but rather it is written: “The entire assembly.” This is an additional emphasis. Since it is so, even if there are one hundred judges, all of them must issue the ruling.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:4.english: One can infer from the language of the Mishna: This sage is liable, but if there was another who acted according to the court's ruling—he is exempt. And why? But indeed, the ruling was not finalized by all the judges, for we said that if not all the judges of the court issued the ruling, it is not called a ruling! And they answer: What are we dealing with here? For example, where that one of them who disagreed with them bowed his head and appeared to agree with them.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:5.english: Come and hear proof from what we learned, which relates to this matter of Rabbi Yonatan: If the court issued a ruling, and one of them knew that they erred and said to them: "You are mistaken"—they are exempt. And we infer: The reason that they are exempt is specifically that he said to them: "You are mistaken." But if he was silent—they are liable, and the ruling is finalized. And why? But not all of them issued the ruling, and if so, this contradicts Rabbi Yonatan's words! They say in response: So too here, it is a case where that one bowed his head.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:6.english: Rav Mesharshiyya raises an objection to the words of Rabbi Yonatan from what we learned: Our Sages relied on the words of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and on the words of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, who would say: One does not issue a decree upon the public unless the majority of the public can withstand it.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:7.english: And Rav Adda bar Abba said about this: What is the verse that teaches this? As it is stated: “With the curse you are cursed, yet you rob Me, the entire nation” (Malachi 3:9), for the entire nation accepted upon itself by oath (“with the curse”) the laws of tithes, and yet they transgressed them. But here it is written: “The entire nation,” and nevertheless, the majority is considered like the entirety, for from this verse our Sages relied that one does not issue a decree unless the majority of the public can withstand it. From this, there is a strong refutation of Rabbi Yonatan. And they agree: Indeed, it is a strong refutation, and his words are rejected.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:8.english: And they ask: If so, rather, now that Rabbi Yonatan's words, which were based on the superfluous word in the verse, have been refuted, what is the meaning of “the entire assembly” that the Merciful One states? What does this emphasis come to teach us? This is what it says: If all the judges are present and decide thus (according to the majority opinion)—it is a ruling, and if not all of them are present—it is not a ruling.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 3b:9.english: Regarding this matter of the judges' session, Rabbi Yehoshua says: When ten judges sit in judgment—the kolar (the chain of those going to be punished) is suspended around the neck of all of them. And they ask: Isn't this obvious? And they answer: This teaches us that even a student before his teacher, if he saw that an error was made and did not correct it—the obligation rests upon him, and he is not permitted to remain silent out of respect for the Rabbi.

Tosafot on Horayot 3a:22:1.hebrew: אלא כי תיבעי לך כו' - צריך עיון: האם היה אפשר לשאול גם לשיטת מאן דאמר בית דין מייתי אם מתו מיעוט ציבור הראשונים ולא נודע כי אם אל אלו החיים, האם אומרים בית דין [חייבים] דמכל מקום הם הורו שלא כדת או לא? והא דנקט מת בית דין ולא נקט הורו בית דין אחר, דלא אפשר כי אם בסנהדרי גדולה:
